topics.title: Start here
topics.heading: System design topics: start here
topics.one_line: Learn the basic ideas of system design, with their good and bad sides.

summary.what: A set of first lessons on common system design ideas.
summary.job: It teaches what each idea is, how people use it, and its pros and cons.
summary.tradeoff: Every choice has a cost. Everything is a trade-off.

topics.title: Study guide
topics.heading: Study guide
topics.one_line: Pick what to study based on how much time you have before the interview.

summary.what: A list of topics to review, based on a short, medium or long interview timeline.
summary.job: It tells you how wide and how deep to study, and how many practice questions to try.
summary.tradeoff: You cannot know everything. What you get asked depends on your experience, job, company, and luck.

topics.title: Interview approach
topics.heading: How to approach a system design interview question
topics.one_line: Four steps to lead an open design interview, from needs to scaling.

summary.what: A four-step plan for answering a system design interview question.
summary.job: You list needs, sketch the design, detail the main parts, then fix slow spots.
summary.tradeoff: Every fix has a cost. Talk about the possible fixes and their trade-offs.

topics.title: Performance vs scalability
topics.heading: Performance vs scalability
topics.one_line: Tell apart a system slow for one user from one slow under heavy use.

summary.what: A service is scalable when added resources raise its performance in the same proportion.
summary.job: Slow for one user is a performance problem. Slow only under heavy load is a scalability problem.
summary.tradeoff: More performance can mean doing more tasks, or handling bigger tasks such as growing data.

topics.title: Latency vs throughput
topics.heading: Latency vs throughput
topics.one_line: Balance the time one task takes against how many tasks finish over time.

summary.what: Latency is the time one task takes. Throughput is how many tasks finish in a set time.
summary.job: It sets a goal: finish as many tasks as you can, with a wait that is acceptable.
summary.tradeoff: Aim for the most throughput that still keeps the wait acceptable.

topics.title: Availability vs consistency
topics.heading: Availability vs consistency
topics.one_line: When the network fails, choose between the latest data and always answering.

summary.what: In a system of many computers, you can promise only two of three things.
summary.job: The three are the latest data, an answer every time, and working through network splits.
summary.tradeoff: Networks fail, so you must handle splits. Then you choose between the latest data and always answering.

topics.title: Consistency patterns
topics.heading: Consistency patterns
topics.one_line: Choose how copies of the same data stay in step for readers.

summary.what: Weak, eventual and strong consistency say when a reader sees a new write.
summary.job: They decide how copies of data are synced, so clients see the same data.
summary.tradeoff: With weak consistency, a reader may miss a new write. Strong consistency copies data at the same time.

topics.title: Availability patterns
topics.heading: Availability patterns
topics.one_line: Keep a service running when a server fails, using fail-over and copies.

summary.what: Fail-over and replication (copying data to other servers) work together for high availability.
summary.job: With fail-over, a standby server takes over when the main server stops responding.
summary.tradeoff: Fail-over needs more hardware and is more complex. New data can be lost if the main server fails first.

topics.title: Domain name system
topics.heading: Domain name system
topics.one_line: Turn a domain name into the IP address of a server.

summary.what: DNS turns a name like www.example.com into an IP address.
summary.job: A client asks DNS which server to contact. Servers and browsers keep answers for a time.
summary.tradeoff: Asking DNS adds a small delay. Kept answers can be out of date.

topics.title: Content delivery network
topics.heading: Content delivery network
topics.one_line: Serve files from servers close to the user.

summary.what: A CDN is a worldwide network of servers that serve your content from places near users.
summary.job: Users get files from a nearby data center. Your own servers handle fewer requests.
summary.tradeoff: It can cost a lot. Content can be out of date until its time limit (TTL) ends.

topics.title: Load balancer
topics.heading: Load balancer
topics.one_line: Share incoming requests across many servers.

summary.what: A load balancer sends each incoming client request to one of your computing resources.
summary.job: It skips broken or busy servers. It also helps remove a single point of failure.
summary.tradeoff: It can become a slow spot. Adding more load balancers makes the setup more complex.

topics.title: Reverse proxy
topics.heading: Reverse proxy (web server)
topics.one_line: One public front door for your internal servers.

summary.what: A reverse proxy is a web server that gives the public one entry to your internal services.
summary.job: It passes each client request to a server that can answer, then returns that answer.
summary.tradeoff: One proxy alone can fail. Adding more proxies makes the setup more complex.

topics.title: Application layer
topics.heading: Application layer
topics.one_line: Run your app's logic on its own servers, apart from the web servers.

summary.what: You can split the web layer from the application layer.
summary.job: You can grow and set up each layer on its own.
summary.tradeoff: Many small, loosely linked services need a new way to build and run them. Microservices make deployment harder.

topics.title: Database
topics.heading: Database
topics.one_line: Where data is stored, and ways to make it handle more load.

summary.what: This part covers two kinds of database: relational (data in tables) and NoSQL.
summary.job: It shows ways to grow a relational database: copies, splitting it up, and tuning.
summary.tradeoff: Copying, splitting by function, and splitting by data all need more hardware and add complexity.

topics.title: Cache
topics.heading: Cache
topics.one_line: Keep earlier results so repeat requests are fast and servers do less work.

summary.what: A cache saves earlier results, so a repeat request can skip the real work.
summary.job: Pages load faster, and servers and databases get less load.
summary.tradeoff: The cache must match the original data, and deciding when to update it is hard.

topics.title: Asynchronism
topics.heading: Asynchronism
topics.one_line: Do slow work in the background, not while the user waits.

summary.what: Asynchronous work means slow jobs run outside the request, not in line with it.
summary.job: A queue holds jobs while workers do them in the background. The user is not blocked.
summary.tradeoff: Queues add delay and complexity. Cheap or real-time work may fit better done at once.

topics.title: Communication
topics.heading: Communication
topics.one_line: Ways that clients and servers send data to each other.

summary.what: This part covers HTTP, TCP, UDP, RPC and REST.
summary.job: It compares how clients and servers send requests and answers.
summary.tradeoff: TCP is reliable but less suited to time-critical use. UDP is less reliable but suits real-time use.

topics.title: Security
topics.heading: Security
topics.one_line: Basic steps to protect data and user input.

summary.what: Security is a big topic. The primer lists only the basics.
summary.job: Scramble stored and sent data. Clean user input to stop attacks that sneak in database commands.
summary.tradeoff: The primer says basic knowledge is likely enough, unless your role needs security skills.

topics.title: Powers of two table
topics.heading: Powers of two table
topics.one_line: A table of powers of two and the sizes they give.

summary.what: A table that lists powers of two with common counts and byte sizes.
summary.job: It helps with quick, rough sums done by hand (back-of-the-envelope).
summary.tradeoff: None stated in the primer.

topics.title: Latency numbers
topics.heading: Latency numbers every programmer should know
topics.one_line: Typical times of common computer actions, for quick rough sums.

summary.what: A table of how long common computer and network actions take.
summary.job: It gives handy numbers for quick, rough estimates.
summary.tradeoff: None stated in the primer.

topics.title: Additional interview questions
topics.heading: Additional system design interview questions
topics.one_line: More design interview questions, each with links to help you solve it.

summary.what: A table of common design interview questions with links to resources.
summary.job: Follow the links to learn how to solve each question.
summary.tradeoff: None stated in the primer.

topics.title: Real world architectures
topics.heading: Real world architectures
topics.one_line: Articles on how real systems are built.

summary.what: A set of articles on how real systems are designed.
summary.job: They help you spot shared ideas, tools, patterns, and lessons learned.
summary.tradeoff: Do not focus on the small details in these articles.

topics.title: Company architectures
topics.heading: Company architectures
topics.one_line: Links to how named companies built their systems.

summary.what: A table of companies, each with links to articles about its architecture.
summary.job: It helps you find design material for a company you care about.
summary.tradeoff: None stated in the primer.

topics.title: Company engineering blogs
topics.heading: Company engineering blogs
topics.one_line: Engineering blogs from many companies, for interview prep.

summary.what: A list of engineering blogs from many companies.
summary.job: It helps you study the designs of companies where you will interview.
summary.tradeoff: Interview questions might come from the same field as that company.

solutions.one_line: Design a service that links bank accounts, reads transactions, and suggests a budget.
Design a site where users paste text and share it through a random link.
Design a cache that saves the results of the latest web server searches.
Design a feature that ranks the past week's best-selling products by category.
Design a service that grows from one user to millions of users on AWS.
Design the data for a social network that finds the shortest path between people.
Design a Twitter timeline and search: post tweets, view timelines, search keywords.
Design a crawler that visits web pages and lets users search what it found.
Design the code for a call center with operators, supervisors and directors.
Design the code for a 52-card deck, then extend it for blackjack.
Design a hash map, a key lookup table that handles clashing keys by chaining.
Design a cache for web query results that drops the least recently used items.
Design a text chat with users, friend lists, and group chats.
Design a multi-level parking lot for motorcycles, cars and buses.
